author: A Robot
objectives: Identify the four chambers of the human heart and describe their roles
Identify the four heart valves and explain how they prevent backflow
Identify the major vessels entering and leaving the heart
Trace the dual-loop (pulmonary and systemic) path of blood through the heart
Explain why the left ventricle has a thicker myocardium than the right ventricle

modules.description: Introduces the gross external anatomy of the heart and identifies the four chambers: right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, and left ventricle.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Locate and name the four chambers of the heart
Distinguish atria (receiving chambers) from ventricles (pumping chambers)
Understand the right/left and superior/inferior orientation of the heart
instructions: Use the Next and Previous buttons to move through the scene.
Observe each chamber as it is highlighted and named.
Note the difference between the thin-walled atria and thicker-walled ventricles.

components.text: The Four Chambers of the Heart

clips.changeMeaning: Establishes the scene with the rotating heart and title so students see the whole organ before chambers are identified.
clips.narration: Welcome to the structural anatomy of the human heart. The heart is a muscular pump roughly the size of your fist. It is divided into four chambers. Let's identify each one in turn.

components.text: Right Atrium: receives deoxygenated blood from the body

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights the right atrium and stops rotation so the student can focus on the receiving chamber on the heart's right side.
clips.narration: This is the right atrium. It is a thin-walled receiving chamber that collects deoxygenated blood returning from the body.

components.text: Right Ventricle: pumps blood to the lungs

clips.changeMeaning: Updates the label to the right ventricle, the pumping chamber below the right atrium.
clips.narration: Below it is the right ventricle. This pumping chamber pushes blood toward the lungs.

components.text: Left Atrium: receives oxygenated blood from the lungs

clips.changeMeaning: Updates the label to the left atrium on the opposite side, the receiving chamber for oxygenated blood.
clips.narration: On the opposite side is the left atrium, which receives oxygen-rich blood returning from the lungs.

components.text: Left Ventricle: thick wall pumps blood to the whole body

clips.changeMeaning: Updates the label to the left ventricle and resumes slow rotation to emphasize its thick muscular wall.
clips.narration: Finally, the left ventricle. Notice how much thicker its muscular wall is. It must pump blood out to the entire body, a job we will explore later.

modules.description: Identifies the four heart valves and the great vessels entering and leaving the heart, and explains how valves prevent backflow.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Name and locate the tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral, and aortic valves
Identify the superior and inferior vena cava, pulmonary arteries and veins, and aorta
Explain how valves enforce one-way flow during the cardiac cycle
instructions: Step through the clips to see each valve and vessel appear.
Watch the valve open and close demonstration.
Note which vessels carry blood toward and away from the heart.

components.sciptDescription: Animates a heart valve opening and closing on a loop to demonstrate one-way flow. Requires a float openCloseTime in seconds for one full open-close cycle (default 2.0) and a float openAngle in degrees the leaflets rotate when open (default 70). Drives the local rotation of child leaflet transforms to swing between closed and open positions repeatedly.

clips.changeMeaning: Reveals the cutaway heart so internal valves become visible and sets up the valve discussion.
clips.narration: Now we look inside the heart. Four valves keep blood moving in one direction. Between each atrium and ventricle sit the atrioventricular valves; at the exit of each ventricle sit the semilunar valves.

components.text: AV Valves: Tricuspid (right) & Mitral (left) prevent backflow into atria

clips.changeMeaning: Activates the demo valve and its flutter animation to show how a valve opens and closes to prevent backflow.
clips.narration: The tricuspid valve guards the right atrioventricular opening, and the mitral, or bicuspid, valve guards the left. Watch how the leaflets open to let blood pass, then snap shut to prevent backflow.

components.text: Semilunar Valves: Pulmonary & Aortic prevent backflow into ventricles

clips.changeMeaning: Updates label to the semilunar valves, distinguishing the pulmonary and aortic valves at the ventricle exits.
clips.narration: The pulmonary valve sits where the right ventricle meets the pulmonary trunk, and the aortic valve sits where the left ventricle meets the aorta. These semilunar valves stop blood from falling back into the ventricles.

components.text: Great Vessels: Red = oxygenated (aorta), Blue = deoxygenated (vena cavae)

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces the great vessels by enabling the aorta and vena cava tubes color-coded red and blue.
clips.narration: Several great vessels connect to the heart. The superior and inferior vena cava deliver deoxygenated blood, shown in blue. The aorta, shown in red, carries oxygenated blood to the body, while the pulmonary arteries and veins link the heart to the lungs.

modules.description: Animates a blood marker tracing the full pulmonary and systemic circuit through the heart, and compares ventricular wall thickness.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace blood through the pulmonary and systemic loops in correct order
Connect each chamber and valve to its place in the circuit
Explain why the left ventricle wall is thicker than the right
instructions: Follow the colored blood marker as it travels through the heart.
Watch the marker change from blue to red as blood is oxygenated.
Compare the left and right ventricle walls in the final clip.

components.text: Step 1: Deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium

clips.changeMeaning: Starts the blood marker as blue at the right atrium to begin tracing the pulmonary loop.
clips.narration: Let's trace a drop of blood. Deoxygenated blood returns from the body through the vena cavae and enters the right atrium.

components.text: Step 2: Through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle

clips.changeMeaning: Moves the marker down through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, advancing the pulmonary loop.
clips.narration: It passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, which contracts to push the blood onward.

components.text: Step 3: Through the pulmonary valve to the lungs; blood is oxygenated

clips.changeMeaning: Moves the marker up and out toward the lungs through the pulmonary valve, then turns it red to show oxygenation.
clips.narration: The right ventricle pumps the blood through the pulmonary valve and pulmonary arteries to the lungs. There it picks up oxygen and turns bright red.

components.text: Step 4: Oxygenated blood returns to the left atrium

clips.changeMeaning: Returns the now-red marker to the left atrium via the pulmonary veins, beginning the systemic loop.
clips.narration: Oxygen-rich blood returns through the pulmonary veins into the left atrium.

components.text: Step 5: Through the mitral valve into the left ventricle

clips.changeMeaning: Moves the marker through the mitral valve into the left ventricle to continue the systemic loop.
clips.narration: It flows through the mitral valve into the left ventricle, the most powerful chamber of the heart.

components.text: Step 6: Through the aortic valve into the aorta to the body

clips.changeMeaning: Drives the marker out through the aortic valve and aorta to the body, completing the systemic loop.
clips.narration: Finally, the left ventricle pumps the blood through the aortic valve into the aorta and out to the entire body, completing the circuit.

components.text: Right ventricle: thin wall, pumps to lungs. Left ventricle: thick wall, pumps to whole body

clips.changeMeaning: Displays the wall-thickness comparison label and resumes rotation to explain why the left ventricle myocardium is thicker than the right.
clips.narration: Now you can see why the left ventricle wall is so much thicker than the right. The right ventricle only pumps blood the short distance to the lungs, but the left ventricle must generate enough pressure to drive blood through the entire body. More work requires more muscle.
